title: AI Is Making Cyberattacks Faster, Palo Alto CEO Warns After Week of Outages
excerpt: Nikesh Arora said a week of outages at Microsoft, the FAA, JPMorgan and Apple was 'not a coincidence.' The operators blame internal faults, not attacks — but Indian experts say AI is compressing attack timelines either way.
body:
• Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora said on X that a week of outages at Microsoft, the FAA, JPMorgan Chase and Apple was "not a coincidence," blaming AI-assisted attacks and a rush of emergency patches.
  • The companies and agencies involved attribute their outages to internal causes — a software defect, a router upgrade, a software bug and an internal update — and none has been established as a cyberattack.
  • Indian security experts told Inc42 that AI is mainly making known techniques faster: error-free phishing, voice cloning, and automated scans that find forgotten systems in seconds.
  • For Indian enterprises, the experts' checklist is concrete: close exposed credentials and unpatched systems, inventory every AI tool staff are using, and rehearse restoring from backups.

A week of outages at some of the world's most critical digital systems — Microsoft, the US Federal Aviation Administration, JPMorgan Chase and Apple among them — drew a pointed verdict from the head of one of the world's largest cybersecurity companies. "So what the industry tried to warn enterprises about six months ago is here. The events of this week so far are not a coincidence. AI is making it easy for hackers to attack multiple customers," Nikesh Arora, chairman and chief executive of Palo Alto Networks, wrote on X early on Wednesday, in a post reported by The S Bharat.

"So what the industry tried to warn enterprises about six months ago is here. The events of this week so far are not a coincidence."

— Nikesh Arora, CEO, Palo Alto Networks

A week of failures, in order

The run began on November 12, when Microsoft Outlook, Teams and Copilot went down for millions of users globally. On November 13, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop after a communications outage, with more than 10,000 flights cancelled or delayed; Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a newly installed router flooded the network with connection attempts, disrupting radar feeds at 17 control centres. On November 16, thousands of JPMorgan Chase customers struggled to access accounts or use cards at ATMs; the bank later confirmed a software bug in its own systems caused the outage. On Tuesday, November 17, Apple and Google users reported problems with iCloud, Apple Pay, Gmail and Google Search.

What the operators say caused them

None of these incidents has been established as an AI-assisted cyberattack, and the operators have given internal explanations for each. Apple said an internal update caused its outage and that it was not a cyberattack, Reuters reported. JPMorgan attributed its failure to a software bug. The FAA pointed to the router installation. Arora's argument is narrower than the headline version: alongside AI-assisted attacks, he blamed some disruption on a "deluge of patches" from vendors rushing to fix vulnerabilities AI systems had discovered, overwhelming IT teams. He urged enterprises to test infrastructure across multiple AI models and rebuild security operations centres to detect and remediate in record time.

What AI actually changes for attackers

Indian security experts interviewed by Inc42 described acceleration more than novelty. Ritesh Bhatia, founder of cybersecurity firm V4WEB, said AI is speeding up techniques attackers have used for years, visibly in three areas: speed, scale and realism. Tasks that took days or months now take seconds to hours; generative AI writes phishing emails without the grammatical errors that once gave them away; voice cloning and deepfakes let attackers impersonate senior executives issuing fraudulent instructions.

Bhatia also flagged "shadow infrastructure" — untracked, forgotten systems outside regular IT monitoring — which AI-assisted scanning can now find and probe quickly. Manohar Reddy Pagilla, a threat researcher at CloudSEK, pointed to scale: "What previously required multiple individuals with specialised skills can now increasingly be handled by a single attacker." Compromising one technology provider that serves hundreds of organisations, he added, can reward an attacker more than targeting each business individually. Yash Kadakia, founder and CTO of Security Brigade, put the symmetry plainly: "The same capabilities that make our security testing faster can also make attackers substantially more effective."

The exposure is also growing from inside: as enterprises hand AI systems customer queries, refunds, code and database access, each integration is a new entry point, and employees' unapproved "shadow AI" tools add more. Akshit Kaushik, cofounder of Mitigata, warned that attackers can hide malicious instructions inside routine emails and documents, manipulating enterprise AI assistants into leaking data or acting without authorisation.

What Indian enterprises are being told to do

For India, where banking, real-time payments, telecommunications, power and public services run on interconnected digital infrastructure, the experts converged on three priorities. First, modernise: Kaushal Bheda of Pelorus Technologies warned that reliance on foreign software and cloud platforms for critical infrastructure adds geopolitical and supply-chain risk, and argued for upgrading legacy systems and investing in indigenous security products. Second, hygiene at speed: Pagilla advised locking down exposed credentials, unpatched internet-facing assets, excessive permissions and vendor weaknesses, and adding external threat intelligence to internal security operations. Third, plan for the breach: Bhatia argued companies must test backups, rehearse restoration and prepare crisis-communication playbooks. "Death, taxes and cyberhacks are bound to happen," he said.

The week's outages may each have had an ordinary cause. The experts' point is that the defence question no longer depends on that distinction: whether failures come from attacks, rushed patches or fragile systems, Indian enterprises now have to detect and recover at the speed AI has set for the other side.
nri_angle: Indian enterprises and the Indian IT firms that run security operations for global clients face the same AI-accelerated attack speeds, with banking and payments infrastructure most exposed.
